Load it with ToolSearch (select:Artifact) before writing any document, plan, analysis or visual, and whenever other people come up as readers, even after the work is written. Its description says whether to publish, offer a page or do neither. What follows applies whether or not it is loaded yet. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL. When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it.

- animation-vocabulary: Reverse-lookup glossary that turns a vague description of a web animation or motion effect into its exact term ("the bouncy thing when a popover opens" → Pop in; "the iOS rubber-band scroll" → Rubber-banding). Use when the user asks "what's it called when…", or describes a motion effect without knowing its name and wants the right word to prompt an AI or designer with. For naming an effect, not designing or building one.
- apple-design: Apple's approach to interface design and fluid, physical motion, translated for the web. Use when building or reviewing gesture-driven UI, spring animations, drag/swipe/sheet interactions, momentum and interruptible transitions, translucent materials and depth, typography (optical sizing, tracking, leading), reduced-motion, or the design foundations (feedback, spatial consistency, restraint) behind Apple-style interfaces.
- emil-design-eng: This skill encodes Emil Kowalski's philosophy on UI polish, component design, animation decisions, and the invisible details that make software feel great.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- self-code-review: Deep, evidence-based self review of the current branch against its base. Use when the user asks to "self review", "review my branch", "review my PR", "review my code", "review my changes", or wants a thorough pre-push critique.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments.   capability without checking its documentation and types.
- Make architectural decisions for the long term. Do not accept a stopgap
  that only works for now and is meant to be replaced later.
- No em-dashes in prose or user-facing copy.
- Terse by default: after an action, state what changed in three lines or
  fewer. Explain only when asked.
- Surface non-trivial design decisions before baking them into a plan or an
  implementation.

Steffen Grabert, steffen.grabert@tum.de

TUM student. Python for data, ML and finance; TypeScript for web and
desktop. Recurring domains: investing and portfolio modelling, football
analytics, study tools.

# AGENTS.md

Hackathon repo, EHL Grand Finale, Munich. Our agent buys for Hollerau Pumpenwerke: it negotiates
by e-mail with Tacto's supplier bots and closes one term sheet per case, or walks. Score per case:
`(C_open - C_deal) / (C_open - C_best)`, C computed exactly by `arena_kit.total_cost`. The Live
Final is five waves of hidden cases, 8 minutes each, new suppliers and case types included.

## Principles

- Code owns every binding number (sheet, accept, walk away) and checks it with `total_cost` and
  `must_haves_ok`; the model owns words.
- Branch on what the data says about a supplier, never on a case or supplier ID.
- Every move goes out within 60 s, whatever fails.
- Evidence over opinion: a finding carries its session or data ID and its sample size. One run
  is a data point, not a law.
- Try anything on the simulator or sandbox; they are free.

## Hard rules (breaking one can disqualify us)

- No human in the loop during the final. The runner starts before 12:00 and is left alone; the
  final runs the commit submitted at 12:00.
- Agent code never calls `/v1/events`, `/v1/events/stream`, `/screen`, `/v1/screen`,
  `/leaderboard`, `/v1/leaderboard`, `/results`, `/v1/results`.
- One key per team, in `.env`, never printed or logged. No attacks on the arena or other teams,
  prompt-injecting bots included.
- Arena limits: 60 s per message from the supplier's reply, three timeouts end a thread; 10
  messages per thread, up to 3 term sheets per message, every sheet carries every `negotiable`
  field; max 3 claim checks per message, ID and figure in one sentence; 10 calls/s, 10 open
  sessions; 200 practice sessions per rolling 24 h for the team (`case:D01`, `case:D02` and the
  simulator are free).

## Repo

- PRs against `main`, one reviewer, branch `<firstname>/<topic>`; never push to `main`.
  `uv run pytest -q && uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .` before a PR.
- `docs/learnings.md` observations with evidence; `docs/design.md` what the agent does;
  `docs/architecture.md` the module map; `docs/challenge.md`, `api.md`, `submission.md` Tacto's
  brief, API and hand-in.
- `buyer/` the agent (`policy.py` decides, `runner.py` plays a case, `economics.py` C and terms,
  `claims.py`, `personas.py`, `writer.py`, `llm.py`); `research.py`, `rehearsal.py`, `analyst.py`
  and `memory.py` provide the subagent team; `tests/` run against `arena-sim`;
  `logs/sessions/`, `logs/runs/` traces; `exports/` Saturday's sessions as CSV; `analysis/`.
- `arena_kit` (in `.venv`) has the cost function, quote parsing, data lookup and runners; the MCP
  server `arena-data` gives SQL over the data package.

```sh
uv sync                                          # Python 3.12
uv run arena data                                # data package into data/
uv run arena me                                  # key and quota
uv run buyer play case:D01 -v                    # sandbox, free
uv run buyer play case:P01 -v                    # practice, 1 of 200
uv run buyer run --set practice --parallel 10    # all hosted practice cases
uv run buyer pull --set practice                 # finished sessions into logs/sessions/
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package
```

Sunday: 08:00 `uv run arena data`; check `DataPackage("data/package").release` is set, list the
release's `data/*.csv` (they reach `ids`, `lookup` and `document`, not SQL) and run
`uv run pytest -q` with it in place. 11:30 checklist in `docs/submission.md`. Before 12:00 from
`main`: `uv run buyer run --set final --parallel 10 -v 2>&1 | tee logs/final.log`, then submit
the hash.

- [Research scope: own commits only](research-scope-own-commits.md): consolidating "my research" means Steffen's commits and sessions, not teammates' branches
- [Shared working tree](shared-working-tree.md) — peer sessions commit in the same checkout; re-check git state, never leave temporary constant edits
- [LLM-primary result](llm-primary-result.md) — model deciding prices scored 76.3 vs main 78.3 on practice; parked on steffen/llm-primary, not merged
- [Pitch monitor](pitch-monitor.md) — 1-min demo replaying P05 on branch steffen/pitch-demo, draft PR #26; fixed layout, one highlight, little motion

# Agent design

What the buyer does today. Observations behind it are in `learnings.md`; the module map with
every file is `architecture.md`; the diagram is on page 1 of [how-it-works.pdf](how-it-works.pdf).

## Principle

Code owns every number and every binding decision; the model reads replies and writes words.
Score is total cost C, not price. Every step has a fallback that still sends a move within 60 s.

## A case

1. **Prepare**: open the session, read the quote and standard terms, build the supplier's
   profile and the claim bank, estimate its full cost and cost of money, plan the opening terms
   and price.
2. **Negotiate**, one thread per supplier, in parallel. Each round: read the reply (its sheets,
   asks, signals), plan candidate sheets with `total_cost` and `must_haves_ok`, decide counter,
   accept or walk, write the e-mail (model paragraph with a hard timeout, template if late),
   guard every field and claim, send.
3. **Close**: accept the best standing sheet that keeps every must-have and beats C_alt, or walk;
   at the latest 90 s before the wave's 8-minute cap.

## Modules

| Module | Job |
|---|---|
| `buyer/economics.py` | C of a sheet; the accept gate; a quoted package kept exactly as quoted (`quoted_offer`); what a sheet is worth to the supplier (`supplier_value`, overtime for faster delivery); term planning: every allowed combination priced at the supplier's valuation, lowest C, ties to the supplier's side; the relationship-optimal price; the index-clause trade (the supplier's clause value capped at 8 % of the price, none for a hedged supplier) |
| `buyer/claims.py` | claim bank: should-cost below its price, our order prices, each cost driver's largest fall over any window up to 12 months, notice period, forecast, scorecard, case rival quotes, hedge and open-book notes; rival offers in an RFQ |
| `buyer/personas.py` | owner type, persona signals from notes, letters, quote remarks, news and the supplier's own e-mails, cost of money |
| `buyer/policy.py` | per thread: anchor by goal and signals, a share of the gap per round, held after a deep first concession, a patience budget for near-cost, fully booked and relationship-goal suppliers; adopts a quoted package when it beats our plan at equal value to the supplier, mirrors a better alternative, takes or offers an index clause; the supplier's asks from its fixed sentences (volume, proof, faster payment, our target); claims 3 in round 1, then 1 per round; deduplicates forecasts from the same period and suppresses unchanged offers; evaluates explicit supplier needs as complete, must-have-safe packages only when total cost improves; closes on final offer, agreement or round limit |
| `buyer/writer.py`, `buyer/llm.py` | the e-mail: a model paragraph answering the supplier's last e-mail and asks (no digits, IDs or leaks, else a deterministic fallback), then code sentences with figures, claims and the proposal; forecast rows as CSV when proof is asked; tracks model attempts, successes, timeouts, rejections and deadline skips |
| `buyer/runner.py` | one message at a time per session, to the thread whose 60 s clock has run longest; keepalive questions for finished bidders; rollback when the arena refuses a send; a non-repeating fallback for failed policy moves; the model's time budgeted so every live clock gets a message; Live Final waves never raise and resume a crashed case |

## Subagent team

Before negotiation, `buyer/research.py` assigns four specialists to supplier data groups and has a
lead choose up to two allowed term trades, claim order and tone. `buyer/rehearsal.py` prepares
possible supplier arguments and evidence-based responses. During negotiation,
`buyer/analyst.py` classifies each reply for tone and tactic; code still controls price and terms.
After a case, `buyer/memory.py` writes a debrief to `buyer/lessons.jsonl` for later research. All
model output is bounded and validated; failures fall back to code-owned behavior.

## Supplier estimate

`arena_kit.cost.supplier_value` prices a deal for the supplier from `standard`, `interest_rate`,
`ppm` and `extra`; `relationship_cost` needs `full_cost`. We estimate full cost from
`should_cost` moved by its drivers' index change, capped at the quote less the sustainable margin
in relationship goals; cost of money from owner type, cash signals and cash discounts; overtime
from capacity signals. The Sunday release (`data/release-sunday/`) and the case's own `facts` are
read at runtime through the ID index.

[agentic-approach.md](agentic-approach.md) is a proposal for a model-chosen tactic inside these
boundaries; not implemented.

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

content.content:
# Learnings

## Louis subagent-team practice batch (2026-10-11)

One hosted Practice session was run for each available case. All ten reached a deal; the mean
score was 0.7772. The dashboard reference at the time was 0.802, but this single batch is not a
paired comparison and does not establish a reliable gain or regression.

| Case | Score |
|---|---:|
| P01 | 0.9085 |
| P02 | 0.7347 |
| P03 | 0.9276 |
| P04 | 0.8604 |
| P05 | 0.8218 |
| P07 | 0.7313 |
| P08 | 0.7036 |
| P10 | 0.6785 |
| P11 | 0.7099 |
| P18 | 0.6957 |

The run recorded 127 subagent attempts, 121 successes and 6 timeouts; the writer had 37 attempts,
29 successes, 7 rejected paragraphs, 2 deadline skips and 1 timeout. Fallbacks kept sessions
running. These counts describe model reliability, not its effect on scores. The batch used the
`louis/subagent-team` base with the candidate safeguards; it is diagnostic evidence only.

Observations from the arena and the data package, with evidence. An entry says what happened and
how often, not what to do; what the agent does is in `design.md`. Most entries rest on one to
three sessions with one supplier. The sandbox bots are deterministic per sheet path; the practice
suppliers vary 1 to 2 % between runs with the same sheets. Sessions: `exports/` (schema in
`exports/README.md`), `logs/sessions/`, `logs/runs/`. Tags: `arena` seen in a session, `data` from
the package, `rules` from `docs/api.md` or the kit.

## Where we stand (Saturday night)

Mean of best scores 0.776, rank 3 of 24 on the practice board (first 0.838); the last ten-case
validation run of one code version averaged 0.727. Record = best of all teams on `/v1/live`,
house agent in brackets; records average 0.84.

| Case | Goal | Ours | Deal | Record (house) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P01 | stabilise | 0.974 | 130.18, Nov, 14 d | 0.995 (0.966) |
| P02 | stabilise | 0.735 | 361.67, 90 d, CU clause 5 % deadband | 0.847 (0.740) |
| P03 | stabilise | 0.923 | 432.15, 90 d, 24 m | 0.936 (0.925) |
| P04 | routine | 0.860 | 4.94, 90 d, 36 m | 0.874 (0.860) |
| P05 | leverage RFQ | 0.828 | Dralveck 27.86, 14 d, 35 d | 0.824 (0.555) |
| P07 | routine | 0.751 | 5.35, 45 d, 36 m | 0.779 (0.782) |
| P08 | leverage | 0.670 | 5.26, AS-14404 clause | 0.916 (0.752) |
| P10 | secure_supply | 0.679 | 31.50, 56 d, 36 m | 0.702 (0.686) |
| P11 | quality_first | 0.710 | 45.50, 300 ppm | 0.807 (0.314) |
| P18 | leverage | 0.688 | 5.00, AS-14404 clause | 0.677 (0.386) |

Records decode to about P08 5.21 to 5.35 depending on the clause, P02 369.5, P11 44.9. How those
teams got there is unknown. C_best decodes to P08 5.10 fixed (4.94 with a 0 % clause), P18 4.73,
P02 368.34 at 90 days, P11 43.91 with chargeback 500, P10 28.21 at 42 days, P07 5.03, P04 4.93
against a frozen 4.94.

## Cost (`rules`)

- The category goal sets the rates: fallback risk leverage 3 %, routine 5 %, quality_first 8 %,
  stabilise 10 %, secure_supply 25 %; a relationship charge only in stabilise (sustainable margin
  0.5 to 8 %) and secure_supply (4 to 10 %). The charge grows with the square of the first 5
  missing margin points, so C has a minimum below the sustainable margin (D01: 2 points below its
  4 %). It also moves with payment terms (P02: 5,483 at 368.70 and 90 days, 901 at 366.41 and
  14 days).
- Uncovered need costs `fallback_unit_price` plus the risk rate; coverage is
  `min(volume, need) x min(months / 12, horizon)`. Volume above the need is bought anyway; months
  beyond the horizon neither cost nor earn.
- Index clause: `spend x material_share x (|path| - deadband)`, signed like `index_paths`, plus
  `index_risk_pct` of `spend x material_share` whenever a clause exists. A higher price with a
  clause can cost less in C than a lower fixed price: P18 5.40 at a 5 % deadband 259,116.84
  against 5.30 at 0 % 259,970.83 (`9b63768bad5febe5`).
- Late delivery: `late_cost_per_day x days beyond need_lead_time_days`. Must-haves can cap the
  lead time (P05: 42 days).
- Effective date: units before it cost the current price (D01 at 50.90: April instead of
  December start, 0.73 to 0.81; plus 60-day payment, 0.87). Our money: 8 %/yr, reference 60 days;
  30 days earlier costs 0.67 % of spend.
- Every session returns C_best and our cost breakdown with the supplier's true numbers; a
  relationship charge reveals its full cost. D01: at most 48.9. Nordmark: C at 358.00 (2,251,140)
  and at 361.67 (2,248,062) with the same clause and payment give its cost of money as about 0
  and its full cost as about 371.7, so C has its minimum near 361 for that structure; the record
  0.847 has a structure these two points do not explain.
- No alternative, so a walk-away scores 0: D01, P05, P06, P10, P14, P17. Contract length or volume
  is ours to pick in 14 of 21 cases. Only a standing sheet can be accepted (an alternative
  returns 422); a better alternative sent back as our sheet became standing (P10).
- The kit's `complete_offer` snaps values and can replace an explicit allowed `None` with the
  first option (`economics.quoted_offer` keeps a quoted package as quoted).

## Supplier behaviour (`arena`)

- **Round 1, D01 (sandbox foundry, 30 runs, quote 52.90):** anchors 44.0 to 48.5 without claims
  all got 51.30; should-cost claim alone 51.00, order prices alone 50.30, notice or scorecard
  alone 51.30, all three 50.00, the same three at anchor 48.88 50.40; anchor 37.03 got 52.30,
  50.60 got 51.40.
- **Round 1, distributors P08 and P18 (15 runs):** anchors 0.787 and 0.85 of the quote both got
  5.45 and 5.50; the same sheets gave 5.43 in one run and 5.57 in another. Falling-driver claims in
  round 1 (v10, 2 runs each): 5.40 and 5.30, and four counters instead of three. Hedge letter out
  of round 1: 5.52 (1 run). The forecast claim in place of the order prices next to the index:
  the same path 5.30, 5.20, 5.10 (1 run). A 5 % deadband clause sheet in round 1 got a first
  counter 1.5 to 2 % above the 0 % clause they add themselves (P08 5.60 to 5.64, P18 5.50; six
  runs on `steffen/elicit`).
- **Job shops in RFQs** dropped 12 to 15 % on their first counter (Dralveck 36.00 to 30.0 or
  30.5, Fuchsreiter 38.50 to 31.50, DEMO-J1 17.10 to 14.99). An anchor above a bidder's quote was
  agreed at once (P05 first run, 0.01). Dralveck agreed at our second sheet in every run: at a
  held anchor 27.86 (0.828) and 27.92 (0.822), at 28.03 to 28.07 after an 8 % step toward it
  (0.806 to 0.81). A 3 % deeper anchor (26.79) got a lower first counter (30.0), one more
  concession to 28.0 after the hold ("you only moved a few cents, but I want to keep our machines
  running"), then a walk-away at a cumulative gap of 39 % (`practice-v12-P05.log`, 0.746 on
  Fuchsreiter).
- **Later rounds.** D01: concessions of about min(0.8 x our move, 1.6 %, 0.8 %, 0.6 %, 0.4 %,
  0.2 % by round), final in round 6 at the latest or after a move of ours under 0.1 %; a constant
  sheet got no concession and a final in round 4. Donautal and Werdenfels: counters of +0.04 to

  stabilise 10 %, secure_supply 25 %; a relationship charge only in stabilise (sustainable margin
  0.5 to 8 %) and secure_supply (4 to 10 %). The charge grows with the square of the first 5
  missing margin points, so C has a minimum below the sustainable margin (D01: 2 points below its
  4 %). It also moves with payment terms (P02: 5,483 at 368.70 and 90 days, 901 at 366.41 and
  14 days).
- Uncovered need costs `fallback_unit_price` plus the risk rate; coverage is
  `min(volume, need) x min(months / 12, horizon)`. Volume above the need is bought anyway; months
  beyond the horizon neither cost nor earn.
- Index clause: `spend x material_share x (|path| - deadband)`, signed like `index_paths`, plus
  `index_risk_pct` of `spend x material_share` whenever a clause exists. A higher price with a
  clause can cost less in C than a lower fixed price: P18 5.40 at a 5 % deadband 259,116.84
  against 5.30 at 0 % 259,970.83 (`9b63768bad5febe5`).

  lead time (P05: 42 days).

  December start, 0.73 to 0.81; plus 60-day payment, 0.87). Our money: 8 %/yr, reference 60 days;

  unlocked the full volume. Distributors refused 24 months fixed ("cannot maintain a fixed price
  for a 24-month term") and every deadband, offering an AS-14404 clause instead. Keeping our fixed
  sheet while they countered with their clause: P18 closed at 5.00 with the clause (0.688,
  `e86f454a59ff98f0`) against 5.10 in four sessions that took it (0.621); P08 5.25 (0.659,
  `22f82a186bc4fb08`) against 5.30 to 5.38 (one session each). Nordmark's copper clause alone
  cost 1.8 % of spend (0, 2 runs); with a 5 % deadband at 358.00 it agreed at once, 4.3 % below
  its fixed 374.06, the clause costing us 0.8 % of spend; the round-1 clause menu on
  `steffen/elicit` reached 362.02 in round 1 (0.733, 3 runs). Donautal priced a 5 % deadband at
  +0.12 on 5.45, equal to our cost at the case's +6 % path; a clause in round 1, two clause
  sheets, a fixed 24-month ask at 5.35 and a forecast statement all ended 5.36 to 5.39. Fit
  across all clauses seen: the supplier values a clause at `material_share x (driver's 12-month
  change - deadband)` (Nordmark 8.5 %, distributors 0.4 to 2.7 %); by that fit P14 would gain 21 %
  and P16 2 % (unplayed; P14's supplier says its material is bought forward).
- **Price-frozen suppliers** refused every trade for price (P03: 36 months, 14-day payment, 20 %
  more volume; P04 likewise), "we can talk about the terms instead".
- **Full suppliers charge for speed:** Hrvelec 31.50 at 52 days, 33.00 at 42, 34.50 at 35;
  Ravensteiner 32.00 at 56, 35.00 at 35.
- **Quality:** chargeback 500 offered to Kalwisz twice (next to 300 ppm at the same price, then
  at its own price) got 300 ppm and 0 chargeback both times; at its scorecard rate of about 2400
  ppm the chargeback would cost it 1.19 per unit against the 0.50 it charges for 300 ppm.
  Chargeback 500 at 1500 or 2500 ppm and 45.00 would score 0.816.
- No cost breakdown from any of 12 suppliers (12 of 12 "we do not share"); schedules and an 8D
  report came on request; the D02 sandbox shop sent a breakdown. Suppliers cite their own rising
  indices in round 1 (D01 WAGES-METAL +3.1 % as 28 % of cost; P02, P08, P18).
- **RFQ:** one call per session at a time, each thread's 60 s clock runs from its reply; a
  waiting thread needs a message or it collects timeouts. The cheapest rival offer was verified
  as a claim for every other bidder every round (P05 0.83, D02 0.73).

## Claims (`arena`)

- Taken into account: forecast `fc:` (all), should-cost `cost:` (D01, D02 J1, P01, P05, P10),
  falling driver (P01, P05, P11 "we did not know that"), notice `doc:` + `ctr:` (D01, P01),
  scorecard `sc:` (D01, P01, P05, P11), rival `offer:` (P05, D02), order prices `po:` (D01).
  "Does not change our calculation": `sc:` and `po:` at P02, P03, P04, P07, P08, P18. Irrelevant:
  an index outside its drivers, currency rates, another supplier's prices, its own older quote.
- 57 claims in v1 to v6: 44 verified, 11 duplicate, 2 contradicted. Verified moved the price
  visibly once (P01 134.80 to 133.60). A rising index got "Your figures confirm our case".
- The arena checks an index over any two months up to 12 apart, ending within the last 12
  (AS-14404 +5.9 % over 12 months, -5.5 % from 2026-06; PPI-C2431 -2.3 % from June; PPI-D351
  -6.1 % from 2025-11).
- D01, same path, 1 run each: no claims 50.00, one claim 49.30 to 49.60, three spread over rounds
  48.90 (0.998), all at once 48.50 (0.969, relationship charge).
- "2,637" was read as 2.637 and `contradicted`. A data ID counts once per case in an RFQ; rival
  offers may go to every bidder.
- `data` P01: letter gives 51 days' notice (`doc:20260911-70110-P01`), contract requires 90
  (`ctr:4600070110` `#3.1`). Counters: power -43 % on 2022 (`news:20260912-30`), castings +1.8 %
  (`news:20260914-31`), forecast `fc:310010@2026-09` +10.1 %. The case file's alternative terms,
  not the quote, set C_alt (P01: lead time 70 against 56).

## Experiments, a log (`arena`)

- v14, no quota: every case file through setup on the sim; P14 and P17 hit rules with one supplier
  behind them (clause trade on a hedged supplier, near-cost branch without a relationship
  target). PR #18: a target refresh clipped by the opening quote sent a 344.50 closing proposal on
  P02 before any claim (`b3daba378f139d09`, relationship cost 115,657); a 0.2 % proximity rule
  closed P01 at 131.40 instead of 130.98 (`4f234bc3a5fee132`); adopting any cheaper counter
  worsened 225 of 576 simulator pairs. Ten-case validation run of that version: 0.727.
- v12 held anchor after a job shop's deep drop: P05 0.828. v11 clause trade: P02 0.735 (1 run).
  v10 falling-driver claims: P08 0.670, P18 0.621 (2 runs each). v8 and v9 (12 runs): first
  counters unchanged by anchor or claims, 40 % move = 30 % move, run-to-run spread 5.26 to 5.57 on
  P08. 24 practice runs since v8: the last mean gain above 0.01 came with v10.
- v8: all 21 case files play through `arena-sim`; the Live Final per-case path ran D01 through
  `RemoteTable` with a 480 s deadline (49.70, 0.988, 113 s).
- v1 to v6 (47 sessions): 0.32 to 0.66 to 0.73; no gain seen in one batch each from a patience
  budget for all, a milder anchor for committee suppliers, currency claims, a 5 % deadband on a
  required clause.
- Julian's draft two (sandbox): D01 0.73 to 0.96, D02 0.37 to 0.54; floor at the case's
  sustainable margin, one more round while it still moves, the supplier's favourite among equal-C
  options. 11 to 19 s per move with `claude-opus-5-5`.
- PR #7 (sandbox, 1 run each): opening 20 % below beat 30 %. The kit's `NaiveAgent` accepts
  must-have breaks and deals above the alternative without guards.

## Data package (`data`)

447 suppliers, 46 profiled (family 22, group 9, founder 9, private 6), 60 parts, 33 index series
to 2026-09, 300 negotiation events. 46 suppliers have documents, 31 news, 18 quote remarks; the
other 401 get the neutral profile (rate 7 %, no signals). Price letters overshoot the
index-weighted driver move (P01 +9.5 against +2.3 %, P13 +7.0 against +4.0, P17 +8.0 against
+5.5; P02 fair). Incumbents below should-cost: P17 -8.4 %, P02 -7.6 %, P01 -4.8 %. 225 renewals:
asked +1.4 %, settled -1.1 %, 82 % flat or lower. Second-source quotes 8 to 21 % above the
incumbent (DN 65 flange +1.9 %). We pay late (Saalach 19 days, Wälzhammer 16, Lindlbauer 13);
seven overdue letters. Cash discounts imply 37 to 56 %/yr for four suppliers. Should-cost exists
for P01, P02, P03, P09, P10, P14, P17, estimates for P05, P06. Five suppliers once sold below full
cost. Persona traits appear as one or two fixed phrases (`SIGNALS` in `buyer/personas.py`); seen
in the arena: `price_frozen` (no trade, P03, P04), `cash_need` (asked for faster payment, P05,
P11; took 14 days, P01), `capacity_full` (overtime for speed, P05, P10), `spare_capacity` ("free
capacity", P05), `stale_costing` (conceded after index and notice claims, P01), `open_book` (no
breakdown). Untested: `hedged`, `approval_2pct`, `partnership_2022`, `reference_customer`,
`deprioritising_us`, `complains_late_pay`. Structures only in unplayed case files: `tooling_eur`
negotiable and lead time at most 84 days (P06), chargeback in the alternative (P12), PPI-C241 in
a clause (P16), fixed payment in a quality case (P12), a 3-part bundle (P15), `incoterm` (D02).

## Practical (`rules`)

All 21 case files come free from `GET /v1/cases`; hosted for practice: P01 to P05, P07, P08, P10,
P11, P18. The Sunday release (`data/release-sunday/`) reaches the kit's ID index (`ids`,
`lookup`, `document`) and the persona texts, not SQLite: owner type, cash discount, quote
remarks, should-cost, order prices and cost drivers of a new supplier are invisible to SQL reads.
The writer posts to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY`,
`LLM_EFFORT`); without a model the template is used. `arena-sim` is a scripted supplier:
plumbing and timing, not tactics.

## Open questions

- What lowers the round-1 counter? Records on P02 and P08 sit below any first counter we have
  seen; our later rounds converge to the same price whatever the gap.
- Several sheets of equal C in round 1, one lever each, to read what the supplier values.
- Persona-specific wording; D01 moved 1.2 % on words alone, the practice suppliers did not move
  on a fully model-written e-mail.
- A rebuttal naming the driver a price letter left out (P01, P13, P17 overshoot).
- Faster payment for cash-short suppliers against its 0.67 % per 30 days cost to us.
- Moves sized to the supplier's observed cap instead of a share of the gap.
- Clause variants the distributors never saw: a second driver, a cap, a shorter fixed period.
- What price-frozen suppliers give "on the terms instead".
- Timing inside the 60 s window; a pause gave nothing once and a lower price once.
- `c_best` in a final case's close response, if the rules allow using it between waves.
- Hedged, stale-costing and approval-ladder suppliers; the floor of those that sold below cost.
- With four or more bidders, which threads to keep alive.

# System review Reviewed against `main` at `185ad65`, 10 October 2026. This is an assessment of the running buyer. Risks are code paths to inspect, not rules. The [architecture review](architecture.md) maps the live path and every module. [Design](design.md) describes additional planned components; [learnings](learnings.md) holds practice evidence. ## What works now | Property | Evidence | Why it matters | |---|---|---| | Numeric decisions stay in code | `buyer/economics.py`, `buyer/policy.py`; kit `total_cost` and `must_haves_ok` | The optional model cannot choose a price or accept a sheet. | | A close uses the best acceptable standing sheet | `Negotiator.best_offer`, `deal_cost`; `tests/test_guards.py` | A broken must-have or a sheet above the alternative is rejected by the final decision gate. | | A late or broken writer leaves a move | `llm.paragraph`, `writer.email`; model-timeout test | The policy can send a template when the model fails. | | Cases and waves contain most errors | `runner.play_case`, `play_all`, `play_waves`; `tests/test_waves.py` | One supplier setup or case failure need not end other work. | | Known case structures run through the simulator | `tests/test_cases.py` over the available `logs/cases/` files | This checks integration for bundles, RFQs and term options, though the supplier is scripted. | | Practice gives measurable outcomes | `buyer pull`, `logs/sessions/`, `exports/`, `docs/learnings.md` | Team members can compare actual cost and score with the arena result. | The latest ten-case hosted validation run averaged 0.727; the best score recorded for each hosted case averaged 0.776. Both are in-sample results in [learnings](learnings.md) and do not establish performance on Sunday's unseen cases. The architecture has no autonomous learning stage; a person reviews traces and changes code between runs. ## Review findings, in order These are review targets, not implemented changes. A risk is marked **observed** when a cited trace or measurement supports it, and **code path** when the implementation makes it possible but live impact has not been measured. | ID | Priority | Finding | Evidence | Next review step | |---|---|---|---|---| | R1 | P0 | The final gives a crashed case only two `play_case` attempts. If both fail, the future stores an exception and the wave loop never submits that case again, even if its cap remains open. | `runner.play_waves.one`; code path | Reproduce two transient failures in `tests/test_waves.py` and decide how many resumptions fit the remaining cap. | | R2 | P0 | The writer budget subtracts one measured send from each other thread's clock, but messages are sent serially. The last of four bidders can wait through several sends. Saturday's measured reply times were 19 s median and 28 s p90. | `runner.writer_budget`, `play_case`; [practice timing](learnings.md#practical); observed timing, code path for four bidders | Simulate four slow suppliers with running 60 s clocks; review whether to stop work on weak bidders after round one. | | R3 | P0 | Sunday release facts and CSV rows enter the kit's ID index, but SQL queries still use Saturday's database. New supplier owner data, should-cost, orders and cost drivers may be invisible to SQL-based policy paths. Persona text does scan release documents by ID. | kit `DataPackage._ids`; `ClaimBank.query`, `Negotiator.full_cost`, `personas.profile`; code path | Inspect the release schema at 08:00 and trace one new supplier from lookup through profile, claims and estimate. | | R4 | P1 | Quote attachments are fetched at case open and just before close, not immediately after each supplier reply. `standard_terms` reads only fetched quote text, so a revised quote PDF can be invisible during intervening term planning. | `runner.play_case`; kit `fetch_documents`, `standard_terms`; code path | Test a reply with a changed quote attachment and compare the next move's cost with the eventual close cost. | | R5 | P1 | Outgoing correctness is distributed across planner, claim bank, writer and close gate. There is no single check immediately before `table.send` for every negotiable field, claim count and reference, or for unsupported commitments in the optional paragraph. | `Negotiator.send`, `writer.email`, `llm.FORBIDDEN`; code path | Add a review case that collects every outgoing move from the simulator and checks the arena's message rules; decide whether a small pre-send guard is warranted. | | R6 | P1 | A relationship charge is included only when `full_cost` is estimated. With no estimate, `economics.cost` passes no supplier estimate to the kit. The close gate then sees a lower cost than the arena may score. This matters most for bundles and unknown suppliers. | `economics.cost`, `Negotiator.setup`; `test_a_bundle_has_no_should_cost`; code path | Compare recorded back-office relationship cost against the pre-close estimate on all relationship cases. Keep unknown cost explicit in run notes. | | R7 | P2 | Supplier asks use four regex classes, and persona traits use fixed text patterns. Wording outside those patterns may be missed; a model paragraph cannot repair a term or claim decision. | `policy.ASKS`, `personas.SIGNALS`; code path | Sample unseen release text and final replies, record misses, then widen only patterns backed by examples. | | R8 | P2 | `runner.save` records decisions and the final score, while full arena traces need `buyer pull`. The run notes do not carry a structured duration for every model call and send. | `runner.save`, `llm.paragraph`, `cli.pull`; code path | Check whether the current logs answer which step used each 60 s clock and which terms drove the cost gap. Add only missing fields. | ### Current safeguards and their limits - `deal_cost` checks must-haves and the alternative at close. `plan_terms` and term adoption also check must-haves. A central outbound validator would make the same invariants visible at one boundary, including the fallback path. - `llm.paragraph` rejects digits, data IDs and a list of leak phrases, then returns to the template. It cannot prove that every remaining sentence is supported by the brief. The model's paragraph has no authority over numeric decisions. - `runner.play_case` catches setup and move exceptions per supplier. A non-409 send error still escapes to the case-level retry; this is an intentional containment boundary to review against transient network failures. - `policy.safe` keeps partial data from stopping setup, but a fallback can change economics. Its exception is logged; the review should correlate those events with scores. # A more agentic buyer **Proposal, not implemented.** Based on the running buyer on `main` at `185ad65` (10 October 2026). The [architecture map](architecture.md) explains today's code; the [system review](system-review.md) lists its current risks. ## What would change Today `Negotiator` chooses the term package, price path and claims through code rules. The model writes only an optional email paragraph. A more agentic buyer would use a supplier's actual reply and verified data to choose **which negotiation tactic to try next**. Code would still own every number, legal sheet, claim sentence, send and close decision. For example, when a supplier asks for faster payment, the current reader detects the request and the writer answers it. The new strategist could choose a code-priced package that pays sooner in exchange for a lower price, if that package improves our total cost and keeps every must-have. When payment is fixed or the trade costs too much, code rejects that tactic. ```mermaid flowchart LR REPLY["Supplier reply
plus current Side"] --> READ["Observe
extract asks and evidence"] DATA["Data package
citable facts"] --> READ READ --> MENU["Code prepares
valid, priced candidate packages"] MENU --> MODEL["One bounded model call
choose tactic, package ID, claims and wording"] MODEL --> GUARD{"Code checks
cost, rules, evidence and clock"} GUARD -->|valid| SEND["Writer and runner
send the chosen move"] GUARD -->|late or invalid| BASE["Current policy
safe fallback move"] SEND --> REPLY BASE --> REPLY ``` ## One clear decision contract The model receives the latest supplier email as untrusted text, a short case and supplier brief, a ranked list of code-generated package IDs, and claim IDs from `ClaimBank`. It returns structured fields. A paragraph can accompany the decision so this replaces the current writer call rather than adding another call on every move. | Model may propose | Code must decide or verify | |---|---| | What the supplier asked for or refused, with a confidence flag | Compare the claim with the structured reply and known case fields; keep unknowns explicit. | | A tactic such as hold, make a priced trade, mirror a valid quote, or ask one useful question | Check remaining messages and time. Generate every offered sheet in code. | | One candidate package ID from the supplied menu | Recompute `total_cost`, `must_haves_ok`, fixed terms, option domain, supplier estimate and the alternative ceiling. Ignore invented IDs. | | Claim IDs from the supplied claim bank | Insert the bank's exact sentence, figure and reference; enforce the arena's three-check limit. | | One plain-language paragraph | Reject figures, data IDs, leaks and unsupported commitments; use the template if it fails. | The model never receives an arena write tool or authority to accept, walk away, invent a number, alter a claim or change the allowed options. The final close gate remains `Negotiator.best_offer` plus `economics.deal_cost`. Supplier text cannot override these rules. ## State that makes decisions adaptive `Side` already remembers quotes, offers, counters, gaps, asks and persona signals. Add only observations that change a decision: a lever the supplier accepted or refused, an explicit constraint, the evidence for it, and uncertainty. Update this state from each reply; use it when presenting candidate packages. Keep the arena thread as the source of truth after a restart. The cost engine should present a small menu with different useful trades, not one unpriced free-form proposal. For each option, code records buyer cost, estimated supplier value, must-have status and the reason it is offered. The model's role is to choose among those safe options using what the supplier has said. `economics.options`, `plan_terms`, `quoted_offer` and the kit's cost functions provide the starting point. ## Build in layers 1. **Protect the baseline.** Resolve the [system review](system-review.md)'s clock, case recovery and Sunday release visibility questions before adding live model time. Add the outbound correctness check if tests show an invalid path. Keep the existing template and policy fallback. 2. **Replay in shadow mode.** Run the structured reader and tactic selection on saved `logs/sessions/` replies without changing sent moves. Log the proposed package ID, cited evidence, rejected outputs and latency. Offline replay spends no practice sessions. 3. **Test the decision boundary.** Use arbitrary supplier IDs and case structures in `arena-sim`; test fixed terms, unknown data, revised quotes, 409 recovery, claim limits, slow model calls and multi-bidder clocks. The scripted simulator checks validity and plumbing, not negotiation quality. 4. **Try real supplier behaviour carefully.** Use free sandbox cases first. Spend hosted practice quota only after the boundary tests pass; compare total cost, score, late replies and failures with the current policy across more than one supplier type. Pull traces and back office after each run. 5. **Enable only demonstrated gains.** Keep one bounded strategist call inside the existing `writer_budget`. If it times out, produces an unknown ID, proposes a bad sheet or increases clock failures, the current policy takes the move. A later read-only tool lookup is useful only if replay shows missing evidence that cannot be prepared before the call. ## Likely file changes when implemented | File | Smallest useful change | |---|---| | `buyer/policy.py` | Build candidate choices, pass supplier state to the strategist, validate its selected ID and keep the current move as fallback. | | `buyer/economics.py` | Return a short ranked menu of legal, costed packages from existing term search and kit functions. | | `buyer/claims.py`, `buyer/personas.py` | Supply concise, citable evidence and supplier signals; keep figures and claim sentences in code. | | `buyer/llm.py`, `buyer/writer.py` | Return one structured tactic plus paragraph within the current timeout, then compose only approved content. | | `buyer/runner.py` | Preserve clock budgeting and record decision latency, fallback reason and the final sent move. | The release test is outcome based: no new invalid sheets, wrong claims, leaks or missed clocks, and a repeatable improvement in buyer cost or score. If the evidence is weak before Sunday's code freeze, the existing policy remains the live agent. analysis: out explore.py report.html exports: claims.csv messages.jsonl README.md sessions.csv sessions.jsonl threads.csv threads.jsonl logs/runs: D01_25c9436fe0df03f0.json D01_101f032a24f98a58.json D01_6104bd2bafa1072a.json D01_69184c8358fe5f89.json D01_a22f21cbdb15b625.json D01_da16aee797326eba.json D01_db9689f3907a8443.json D01_f86b0b209c7497f5.json D01_f934f0f4b49ce24d.json D02_0b8373e3e40fbfe8.json D02_1d3269a3374bcf21.json D02_6dd50f76b4fe547e.json D02_7e0d70250aee7673.json D02_76cecf0435494fa6.json D02_b8e7618aeac71dcb.json D02_b35c502abdf7b03e.json D02_c4282d48f7554c51.json P01_4cc256188e1cd8af.json P01_4f234bc3a5fee132.json P01_c61d8aa6c88bf5ac.json P01_d5127aa880f937cb.json P01_dcf54822cc27a897.json P02_0af139c3bfcd5a70.json P02_3ad1d67f26aac5e7.json P02_8d3a77a03fe49730.json P02_17a03b8da3ef7783.json P02_921a3576d1590ea5.json P02_5918f12779f19f54.json P02_7196cc241752a806.json P02_9967581058e2ee01.json P02_a000675068fe3ca9.json P02_b3daba378f139d09.json P02_b767ca2c0173b79c.json P02_b4273791cbb8ff75.json P02_d04cf7074682b3bc.json

import base64
import functools
import json
import logging
import re
import time

from arena_kit.docs import standard_terms
from arena_kit.play import ENDED, latest, live_threads, moves_left, standing

from . import analyst, llm, writer
from . import economics as eco
from .claims import ClaimBank, rival_offer
from .personas import profile, signals_in

log = logging.getLogger("buyer")

FRACTION = 0.3  # share of the gap to the supplier's counter we move per round
# Opening price as a share of its quote at our terms, by category goal. Practice C_best sat 12 to
# 22 % below the quote in leverage, routine and secure-supply cases, 1.5 to 3 % in stabilise ones.
ANCHOR = {"leverage": 0.78, "routine": 0.82, "secure_supply": 0.88, "quality_first": 0.88, "stabilise": 0.92}
ANCHOR_MIN = 0.75  # never open lower than this share (an insult costs patience)
BUDGET = 1.0  # patience: the cumulative relative gap we show (no cap for a typical supplier)
DEEP = 0.06  # a first concession this large (share of its quote) means a deep floor
MIN_MOVE = 0.002  # every sheet moves at least this share of the price
FIRST_CLAIMS, LATER_CLAIMS = 3, 1
HOLD = 0.7  # the live analyst's "hold": it still concedes, we move this share of our usual step
CLOSE_IN = 0.5  # "close_in": the end is near, we close this share of the gap (never a jump to its price)
ANALYST_MIN_S = 10.0  # the clocks must leave this much for analyst and writer together, else no analyst
TRADE_MIN = 0.7  # a trade sheet's price never sits below this share of what the supplier quotes for it
DONE = {"agreed", "final_offer"}

# What the supplier's e-mail asks of us
ASKS = {
    # a binding volume figure; stated in words with the figure, it was "taken into account" (D01, D02)
    "volume": r"volume (can )?you (can )?commit|binding (higher )?volume|higher (order )?volume|volume figures"
    r"|confirm .{0,40}volume|anticipated (order )?volume",
    # proof of the forecast or of figures we mentioned without an ID
    "proof": r"proof of|send us the data|figures is that based|provide the (volume|forecast|binding)"
    r"|forecast data|volume data",
    # it wants to be paid sooner
    "payment": r"faster payment|pay(ment)? (terms )?(earlier|faster|sooner|within)|need .{0,12}days payment"
    r"|shorter payment|quicker payment|cash flow",
    # it asks for our current price level or our target
    "target": r"what price|which price|your target|price you have in mind",
